small_guidance:
- The matmul is M=128, N=32768, K=32768 — very skinny in M. Add autotune configs with BLOCK_M=16/32 and BLOCK_N=256, BLOCK_K=64/128, num_warps=8, num_stages=4 to better saturate the K loop. Drop the BLOCK_M=128 configs (only 1 m-tile possible).
- Use `tl.dot(a, b, out_dtype=tl.float32)` and ensure both operands are loaded as fp16/bf16 if acceptable; otherwise at minimum, drop the K-tail mask by padding/asserting IN_FEATURES % BLOCK_K == 0 (it is, 32768 divisible) — replace masked loads in the K loop with unmasked loads to cut load overhead.
- For stage2, N_GROUPS=16384 is small — use a single-block persistent reduction (BLOCK=16384, num_warps=8, stages=2) with one program per batch row, no outer loop.
large_guidance:
- Fuse all three stages into a single kernel: one program per batch row (or small M-tile) that streams the K dimension and, for each BLOCK_N tile of output, computes matmul+bias, applies max-pool of size 2, sums into a per-row scalar accumulator, and finally scales and stores. This avoids materializing the [B, OUT_FEATURES] or even the [B, N_GROUPS] intermediate, turning a 4GB+ write/read into register-resident accumulation.
- Since M=128 is tiny, consider a split-K / split-N strategy: grid = (B, num_n_splits), each program handles one row × a chunk of N, computes partial pooled-sum, then a tiny final kernel sums the splits and scales. This exposes far more parallelism than 128×(N/BLOCK_N) tiles when BLOCK_N is large.
- Load the weight in bf16/fp16 (cast once at init) to halve K-loop bandwidth; accumulate in fp32. With K=N=32768, this kernel is bandwidth-bound on weight reads, so reducing weight footprint is the highest-leverage change.
